lessons.title: Cells: The Tiny Building Blocks
body: Your body is built from tiny pieces called cells. A cell is so small that you need a microscope to see it, and your body has trillions of them. Cells are the smallest parts of you that are alive.

A cell is a bit like a tiny workshop. A thin skin called the membrane wraps around it and lets in food and oxygen while keeping out things that do not belong. The nucleus is the control room. It holds DNA, which is a set of instructions for how to build and run you. Small parts called mitochondria turn food and oxygen into energy the cell can use.

Not all cells look the same, because they have different jobs. Red blood cells are small discs that carry oxygen. Nerve cells are long and thin so they can send messages. Muscle cells can get shorter, and that is how you move. Skin cells make a tough cover for your body.

Cells also make copies of themselves. That is how you grow taller, and how a scraped knee heals. Groups of the same kind of cell form tissues, tissues join to make organs like the heart, and organs team up in body systems.

lessons.title: Bones and Muscles: Frame and Motion
body: Inside you is a frame called the skeleton. An adult has around 200 bones. Bones hold you up, protect soft parts, and make blood cells inside the soft middle of some of them. The skull protects the brain, and the ribs form a cage around the heart and lungs.

Bones are alive. They are hard because they contain minerals such as calcium, and they can grow and mend. If a bone breaks, new bone grows across the gap, and a doctor may use a cast to hold the pieces still while this happens. Children eat foods with calcium, such as milk, yogurt, beans and leafy greens, and get active play to build strong bones.

Bones cannot move by themselves. Muscles attached to them do the work. A muscle can only pull, never push, so muscles work in pairs. When the muscle on the front of your upper arm gets shorter, your elbow bends. When the muscle on the back gets shorter, your arm straightens.
You also have muscles you do not control on purpose. Your heart is a muscle that beats all day and night, and muscles in your stomach squeeze food along without you thinking about it.

lessons.title: The Heart and Blood
body: Your heart is a strong muscle about the size of your fist. It works as a pump. Each squeeze pushes blood into tubes called blood vessels, which carry it to every part of your body and back again.

Blood is a delivery service. Red blood cells carry oxygen from the lungs. Blood also carries food energy to cells and carries away waste. White blood cells help fight germs. Platelets are tiny pieces that help blood clot, so a small cut stops bleeding.

There are three main kinds of vessels. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, and their walls are thick and stretchy. Veins carry blood back to the heart. Capillaries are the tiniest tubes, thinner than a hair, and they are where oxygen and food pass into the cells.

You can feel your heart at work. Press two fingers gently on the inside of your wrist and you will feel a pulse. That beat is each squeeze of the heart. When you run, your muscles need more oxygen, so your heart beats faster. When you rest, it slows down again.

lessons.title: Lungs and Breathing
body: Your cells need oxygen to release energy from food. You get oxygen from the air by breathing. Air goes in through your nose or mouth, down the windpipe, and into two lungs inside your chest.

Inside each lung, the air tubes split again and again, like branches of a tree. At the very ends are millions of tiny air sacs. The walls of the sacs are very thin and are wrapped in capillaries. Oxygen passes from the air into the blood there. At the same time, carbon dioxide, a waste gas made by your cells, passes out of the blood into the air sacs, and you breathe it out.

Lungs do not have muscles of their own. A large dome-shaped muscle under them, called the diaphragm, does the work. When it tightens and moves down, your chest gets bigger and air flows in. When it relaxes, air flows out.

You can keep your lungs healthy by staying away from cigarette smoke, being active so that your lungs get a good workout, and washing your hands to avoid colds. Mucus and tiny hairs in your airways trap dust and germs so they do not reach the air sacs.

lessons.title: Digestion: From Bite to Energy
body: Food is too big for your cells to use as it is, so your body breaks it into very small pieces. This is called digestion. It starts in your mouth, where teeth chew the food and saliva begins to soften it and break it down.

When you swallow, the food moves down a tube called the esophagus. Muscles in its walls squeeze in waves, so the food gets pushed along even if you were upside down. The food then arrives in the stomach, a stretchy bag that mixes it with strong juices and turns it into a thick liquid.

Most of the digesting finishes in the small intestine, a long, coiled tube. It is called small because it is narrow, not because it is short. It is several meters long. Here the tiny pieces of food, called nutrients, pass through the walls into the blood. The liver and pancreas help by adding juices.

What your body cannot use goes on to the large intestine, which soaks up water. The leftovers leave the body as solid waste. Your kidneys do a different cleaning job: they filter your blood and make urine.

lessons.title: The Brain and Nerves
body: Your brain is the control center of your body. It lets you think, remember, feel, and decide. It also runs jobs you never think about, like keeping your heart beating and your lungs breathing.

The brain has three main parts. The large top part, the cerebrum, is used for thinking, memory, and choosing to move. The cerebellum, at the back, helps with balance and smooth movement. The brain stem connects to the spinal cord and controls breathing and heartbeat.

The spinal cord is a thick bundle of nerves that runs down the middle of your back inside the bones of the spine. Nerves branch from it across the whole body, a little like wires. Messages travel along nerve cells as tiny electrical signals, very fast.

Here is an example. You touch something hot. Nerves in your fingers send a signal to your spinal cord, and a reflex pulls your hand away before the brain has even finished noticing the pain. Reflexes protect you because they are quick. You protect your brain by wearing a helmet when biking and by getting enough sleep.

lessons.title: Skin: Your Body's Cover
body: Your skin is an organ, and it is the largest one you have. It covers your whole body and does several jobs at once.

First, skin is a barrier. The outer layer is made of tough, flat cells that keep water in and keep most germs out. Skin cells on the outside wear off and are replaced by new ones from below, so your skin renews itself all the time.
Second, skin helps keep your temperature steady. When you are hot, you sweat, and as the sweat dries it cools you down. When you are cold, the tiny blood vessels in the skin narrow to save heat.
Third, skin senses. It holds nerve endings that tell your brain about touch, pressure, heat, cold and pain. Pain is useful, because it warns you to move away from danger.

Skin also contains a coloring called melanin, which gives skin its shade and offers some protection from the sun. Everyone, whatever their skin shade, needs shade, a hat or sunscreen to protect against sunburn. If skin is cut, the body clots the blood and closes the gap, and a clean bandage helps keep germs out while it heals.

lessons.title: The Senses
body: Your senses gather information about the world. You have five main ones: sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch. Each sense has special cells called receptors that turn what they detect into signals for the brain.

In the eye, light enters through the clear front and is focused by a lens onto the retina at the back. The retina has cells that notice light and color. The optic nerve carries those signals to the brain, and the brain builds the picture. If the focus is off, glasses can help bend the light correctly.

Sound is vibrations in the air. The outer ear funnels the vibrations to the eardrum, which shakes. Three tiny bones pass the shaking to the inner ear, where hair cells change it into nerve signals. Very loud noise can damage these hair cells for good, so protect your ears.

Smell and taste work together. Your nose detects tiny particles in the air. Your tongue has taste buds that detect sweet, salty, sour, bitter and savory. That is why food seems to have little flavor when your nose is stuffy from a cold.
The brain combines all this information so you can react, learn and enjoy the world.

lessons.title: Germs: Tiny Things That Can Make Us Sick
body: Germs are living or almost-living things so small that you need a microscope to see them. Many tiny organisms are harmless or even helpful. Some bacteria in your intestines help you digest food. But some germs can make you sick.

There are two main kinds of germs. Bacteria are single cells that can live and multiply on their own. Strep throat is caused by bacteria. Viruses are even smaller and cannot multiply without getting inside a living cell. Colds and the flu are caused by viruses.

Germs spread in a few ways. Some travel in tiny droplets when a person coughs or sneezes. Some are passed when you touch a surface or a person that has them, then touch your eyes, nose or mouth. Some are in spoiled food or dirty water.

You can block germs. Wash your hands with soap and water for about twenty seconds, especially before eating and after using the bathroom. Cough or sneeze into your elbow. Stay home when you are sick so that you do not pass it on. Keep food at safe temperatures.
Medicine matters here, too. Antibiotics can kill bacteria, but they do not work on viruses, so a doctor decides when they are needed.

lessons.title: The Immune System and Vaccines
body: Your immune system is a team of cells and organs that defends you from germs. Skin and the mucus in your nose are the first walls. If a germ gets past, white blood cells go to work. Some of them swallow germs. Others make proteins called antibodies that stick to a particular germ and mark it for removal.
When you get sick, you may feel a fever, which is a higher body temperature. Fever is one way the body fights, although a very high fever or one that lasts should be checked by a doctor.
The immune system has a memory. After it has beaten a germ once, it remembers it, so if the same germ comes back, the defenders act faster. That is why you usually get chicken pox only once.

Vaccines use this memory. A vaccine shows the immune system a harmless piece or weakened form of a germ, so the body practices without becoming seriously ill. Later, if the real germ arrives, the defenders are ready. Vaccines have greatly reduced diseases such as measles, polio and whooping cough. Like any medicine, vaccines can cause side effects, usually mild ones like a sore arm. Doctors and scientists keep studying them for safety.
Which vaccines you get, and when, is decided with a doctor and your family.

lessons.title: Nutrition: Fueling the Body
body: Food gives your body energy and the materials to grow and repair. The parts of food that your body uses are called nutrients. The main groups are carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and water.

Carbohydrates, found in bread, rice, fruit and potatoes, are the body's main quick fuel. Proteins, in beans, eggs, fish, meat and nuts, are used to build and repair muscles and other cells. Fats store energy and help the brain and body, and we need some of them. Vitamins and minerals are needed in small amounts for jobs such as keeping bones strong, helping blood carry oxygen, and helping you see in dim light.

No single food has everything, so eating a variety is the best plan. Fruits and vegetables of many colors, whole grains, protein foods and dairy or other calcium sources make a balanced plate. Foods high in added sugar, salt or unhealthy fat are fine once in a while but should not be most of what you eat.
Water is just as important. Your body is mostly water, and you lose some every day. Drinking water throughout the day is better for you than sugary drinks.
Some people have food allergies, when the immune system reacts strongly to a food such as peanuts. They must avoid it and tell adults about it.

lessons.title: Exercise and Moving Every Day
body: When you exercise, your muscles work harder, so your heart beats faster and you breathe deeper. Over time, regular activity makes the heart and lungs stronger, so they do the same work with less effort.

Exercise helps in many other ways. Weight-bearing activities such as running, jumping and dancing help bones grow strong. Muscles become stronger. Activity helps keep a healthy body weight, and it often improves mood and helps you sleep better. Many people find that a run or a game outside makes worries feel smaller.

Health organizations such as the World Health Organization suggest that children and teenagers get about an hour a day of moderate to vigorous activity. It does not need to be all at once. Walking to school, playing tag, riding a bike, swimming or joining a team all count. Choose things you enjoy, because you are more likely to keep doing them.

Stay safe while you move. Drink water, wear a helmet for biking or skating, and warm up before hard activity. If something hurts in a sharp way, stop and tell an adult. It is also fine to take rest days, because muscles get stronger while they recover.
Limiting long stretches of sitting, including screen time, gives your body more time to move.

lessons.title: Sleep: Your Body's Repair Time
body: Sleep is not wasted time. While you sleep, your body is busy. Your brain sorts what you learned during the day and stores important memories. Your body repairs itself, and children release growth hormone during deep sleep, which helps them grow.

Sleep happens in cycles. During light sleep your body relaxes. During deep sleep it is hard to wake you and much of the repair work happens. During a stage called REM sleep, the brain is very active and most vivid dreams happen. A full night includes several of these cycles.
Health groups say that school-age children generally need about nine to twelve hours of sleep each night, and teenagers need about eight to ten. Needs differ a little from person to person.
Not enough sleep can make it hard to pay attention, learn, and control feelings. People who are tired may feel cranky and may catch more colds.

Good sleep habits help. Go to bed and wake up at about the same time each day. Keep your room dark, cool and quiet. Turn off screens for a while before bed, because the light and exciting content can make it harder to fall asleep. If worries keep you awake, tell a trusted adult.

lessons.title: Growing Up and Puberty Basics
body: All living things grow and change, and humans do so for many years. Between roughly ages 8 and 14, most children begin puberty, the time when the body changes from a child's into an adult's. Puberty is controlled by hormones, which are chemical messengers made by glands. They travel in the blood and tell parts of the body what to do.

Some changes happen to nearly everyone. You grow taller quickly, sometimes in sudden spurts. Body hair grows in new places, and sweat becomes stronger smelling, so washing daily and using deodorant can help. Skin may become oily, and pimples are common. Feelings can swing up and down more than before.

Other changes are different for different bodies. In girls, breasts start to develop and menstruation, or a period, begins, usually around ages 10 to 15. In boys, the voice deepens, the shoulders broaden, and the testicles and penis grow. These changes are part of how the reproductive system prepares for adulthood.
The most important fact is that the timing varies. Some people start early and some start later, and both are normal. There is no right schedule, and comparing yourself with friends is not helpful.

Questions about puberty are good ones. A parent, caregiver, school nurse or doctor can give you accurate answers. Your body belongs to you, and you can always tell a trusted adult if anything makes you feel unsafe.

lessons.title: Mental Health and Coping
body: Mental health means how you think, feel and handle life. Just as you can have a cold in your body, your mind can have hard times too. Everyone has feelings such as joy, anger, fear and sadness. None of them is bad. Feelings give information, and what matters is what we do with them.

Healthy ways to cope include naming the feeling out loud, taking slow deep breaths, going for a walk or playing, drawing or writing, listening to calming music, and talking to someone you trust. Breathing slowly works because it helps calm the body's alarm response. Getting enough sleep, eating regularly and being active also support a steady mood.

Sometimes feelings are too big or last too long. If you feel sad or worried for weeks, cannot enjoy things you used to, have trouble sleeping or eating, or feel you want to hurt yourself, that is a sign to tell a trusted adult right away. Doctors, school counselors and therapists are trained to help, and many problems such as anxiety and depression can be treated. Asking for help is a strength, not a weakness.

You can also help others. If a friend seems very sad, listen kindly and encourage them to talk to an adult. If a friend ever talks about hurting themselves, tell an adult immediately even if they ask you to keep it secret. In the United States, the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline can be reached by calling or texting 988.

lessons.title: First Aid: Cuts, Burns and Calling for Help
body: First aid is the quick help you give before a doctor or ambulance arrives, or care for a small injury. The first rule is safety: if the place is dangerous, do not put yourself in danger, and get an adult.

For a small cut or scrape, wash your hands first if you can. Press a clean cloth on the cut to stop the bleeding, which can take a few minutes. Rinse the cut gently with clean water, then cover it with a clean bandage. Tell an adult. If blood is spurting, will not stop, or the cut is deep, call for help right away.

For a small burn, cool it under cool running water for several minutes. Do not use ice, butter or oil. Cover it loosely with a clean cloth and tell an adult. A burn that is large, blistered over a big area, or on the face or hands needs a grown-up and medical help.

Know how to call for help. In the United States the emergency number is 911. Other countries have their own numbers, so learn yours. Stay calm, say your name and where you are, tell what happened, and answer the questions. Do not hang up until the call taker says you can.
Call for help if someone is not breathing, will not wake up, has a bad injury, is choking and cannot speak, or has a serious allergic reaction.

lessons.title: Medicine Safety
body: Medicines are substances that treat, prevent or relieve illness. Used properly, they help a great deal. Used the wrong way, they can be dangerous, even if they come from a store and even if they look like candy.

Here are the main safety rules. Only take medicine that a parent, caregiver, doctor or nurse gives you, and never take it alone. Take the amount the label or doctor says, because more is not better and can cause harm. Never share your medicine with someone else, and never take someone else's, because medicine is chosen for a particular person.

Read the label together with an adult. It lists what the medicine is for, how much to take, when to stop, and warnings. Check the expiration date. Keep medicines in their original container, in a safe place that young children cannot reach, such as a locked cabinet.

If you or a child swallows a medicine or a household product by mistake, tell an adult right away. In the United States, Poison Control can be reached at 1-800-222-1222, and 911 is for serious emergencies. Do not wait for symptoms.
Vitamins and cough syrups count as medicines, too. When you finish a course of antibiotics, the doctor decides how long to take them, so do not stop early or save leftovers.

lessons.title: Doctors, Nurses and Scientists
body: Many people work to keep us healthy. A doctor, also called a physician, studies for many years to learn how the body works and how illness is found and treated. Some doctors are general, like a pediatrician who cares for children. Others are specialists, such as a cardiologist for hearts or a surgeon who operates.

Nurses give care and teach patients. They check things like temperature and heartbeat, give medicines as ordered, comfort people, and notice when something changes. Other helpers include dentists, who care for teeth, pharmacists, who prepare medicines and explain how to use them, physical therapists, who help people move after an injury, and paramedics, who give emergency care.

Scientists work behind the scenes. Researchers study germs, test new treatments, and learn why diseases happen. They use the scientific method: ask a question, test it carefully, and check the results. For a new medicine, careful studies called clinical trials test whether it works and is safe before it is approved for use.

When a check-up happens, a doctor may ask about your health, listen to your heart and lungs, and check growth. It is a good time to ask questions. Going to a doctor when healthy helps prevent problems.
You can be a health helper too, by washing hands, eating well and being kind to a friend who is not well.

questions.prompt: Which part of a cell holds the DNA, the instructions for building and running the body?
choices: The nucleus, which works like the control room of the cell
The membrane, which wraps around the outside of the cell and guards it
The mitochondria, which make energy for the cell to use up each day
The red disc, which carries oxygen through the blood to the organs

questions.prompt: What do mitochondria do inside a cell?
choices: They help the cell make a copy of itself when you grow
They turn food and oxygen into energy that the cell can use
They store the instructions that tell the cell how the whole body is built
They decide which things may enter or leave the cell wall

questions.prompt: Why are nerve cells long and thin, while red blood cells are small round discs?
choices: Red blood cells have no nucleus because they are not alive
All cells start out the same and then change shape by chance
Each kind of cell has a shape that fits the job it does
Nerve cells grow older and stretch out over many years

questions.prompt: Your knee is scraped and a few days later new skin has grown. Which cell activity explains this?
choices: Muscle cells from deep under the skin change into skin cells and cover the area
The nucleus leaves the damaged cells and moves away
Blood cells turn into bone cells to cover over the wound
Cells make copies of themselves to fill in the damaged spot

questions.prompt: Which of these is a job of the skeleton?
choices: It carries oxygen from the lungs to every cell in the body
It breaks down food into tiny pieces that you can then use
It sends fast messages from the brain down to the toes
It holds you up and protects soft parts like the brain

questions.prompt: What can a muscle do?
choices: It can only push, which is why we need bones to pull
It can slide bones along the ground without any bending
It can only pull by getting shorter, so it cannot push
It can both push and pull by growing longer and shorter

questions.prompt: When the muscle on the back of your upper arm gets shorter, what happens at the elbow?
choices: The arm bends, because the front muscle gets longer and pushes
The arm straightens, because the pair pulls the other way
The arm bends, because both muscles pull in one direction
The arm stays still, because bones cannot be pulled at all

questions.prompt: A child wants strong bones for the future. Which habit best helps?
choices: Eating foods with calcium and getting active, weight-bearing play
Resting in bed all day so that the bones are never used or worn out by play
Drinking only juice so the body has plenty of sugar for bones
Avoiding the sun and the playground so no bone gets hurt

questions.prompt: What do arteries do?
choices: They are the tiniest tubes where oxygen reaches cells
They make the platelets that help a cut stop bleeding
They carry blood away from the heart to the body
They carry blood back to the heart from the body

questions.prompt: What is the main job of red blood cells?
choices: Fighting the germs that get into the body through a small cut
Helping the blood to clot so that bleeding slows down quickly
Making the heart muscle squeeze again and again without rest
Carrying oxygen from the lungs to cells around the body

questions.prompt: After running hard, your pulse is faster. What is the best explanation?
choices: Your working muscles need more oxygen, so the heart pumps faster
Your heart is damaged by the exercise and is struggling to keep up its beat
Your blood has stopped moving and needs to be pushed harder
Your lungs are empty, so the heart takes over the breathing

questions.prompt: Where do oxygen and food pass out of the blood and into body cells?
choices: Through the pulse you can feel at your wrist or your neck
Through the thin walls of the tiny capillaries
Through the thick walls of the big arteries near the heart
Through the one-way flaps found inside the heart chambers

questions.prompt: Which gas do your cells make as waste that you breathe out?
choices: Calcium
Carbon dioxide
Oxygen
Helium

questions.prompt: Which muscle does most of the work of moving air in and out?
choices: The diaphragm, a dome-shaped muscle under the lungs
The biceps, a muscle at the front of the upper arm that bends it
The heart, which squeezes air through the lungs with each beat
The lungs, which have strong muscles of their own for breathing

questions.prompt: Why are the walls of the tiny air sacs very thin and wrapped in capillaries?
choices: It keeps the air trapped inside the sacs so that none of it is ever lost
It stops germs from ever being able to enter the body
It helps the sacs squeeze air along like stomach muscles
It lets oxygen pass into the blood and carbon dioxide pass out

questions.prompt: Which choice best helps keep your lungs healthy?
choices: Breathing only through your mouth during every cold
Staying indoors so that the lungs never have to work
Staying away from cigarette smoke and being active often
Holding your breath for a long time each day to make the lungs stronger

questions.prompt: In which organ does most digestion finish and most nutrients pass into the blood?
choices: The small intestine, a long narrow coiled tube
The esophagus, the tube that carries swallowed food
The large intestine, which soaks up leftover water
The kidney, which filters the blood and makes urine

questions.prompt: What does the stomach do to food?
choices: It chews the food into small bits with the help of saliva
It mixes the food with strong juices into a thick liquid
It soaks up water and turns the leftovers into solid waste
It filters the blood and removes extra water as urine

questions.prompt: Why can a person swallow food and have it reach the stomach even while upside down?
choices: Saliva is so slippery that food slides into the stomach alone
The stomach pulls the food in by breathing in like the lungs
Muscles in the esophagus squeeze in waves and push food along
Gravity pulls food down the esophagus whichever way you are

questions.prompt: What is the job of the kidneys?
choices: They break food into small nutrients with strong stomach juices
They pump blood through the arteries to the whole of the body
They add juices to the small intestine to help in digestion
They filter waste and extra water out of the blood as urine

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain mostly helps with balance and smooth movement?
choices: The cerebrum, the large top part used for thinking
The spinal cord, which runs down the back inside the spine
The optic nerve, which carries signals from the eye
The cerebellum, found at the back of the brain

questions.prompt: How do messages travel along nerve cells?
choices: As air that is pushed through the nerve by the lungs
As food pieces carried to the brain by digestion
As tiny electrical signals that move very quickly
As blood that is pumped along the nerve by the heart

questions.prompt: You touch a hot pan and your hand jerks away before you feel pain. What best explains this?
choices: Your skin cells moved the hand away because they became hot
A reflex through the spinal cord acts faster than conscious thought
Your hand muscles decided on their own to pull away, without using any nerves
Your brain waited until it had thought carefully about the heat

questions.prompt: Which habit best protects the brain?
choices: Wearing a helmet when biking and getting enough sleep
Skipping sleep so that the brain can have more time awake
Riding fast without a helmet because bones protect the brain
Staying indoors so the brain will not have to learn new skills

questions.prompt: What is one job of skin?
choices: It breaks down food into pieces the blood can carry
It stores DNA in a control room at its centre
It keeps water in and most germs out as a barrier
It pumps blood to every part of the body all day

questions.prompt: How does sweating help the body?
choices: It adds a layer of warmth that protects against the cold
It washes the germs out of the body through the blood
It turns the extra water into the pigment called melanin
As sweat dries on the skin it cools you down

questions.prompt: Why is pain, though unpleasant, useful?
choices: It warns the brain of danger so you can move away from harm
It tells the body to stop making new skin cells so the hurt spot can rest
It shows that the skin has no nerve endings left to feel
It helps blood clot by making the heart beat more slowly

questions.prompt: Two friends have different skin shades. What should both of them do on a very sunny day?
choices: Stay in the sun all day to help the skin get thicker
Use shade, a hat or sunscreen, since any skin can burn
Only the lighter-skinned friend needs any kind of sun care
Neither needs care, since melanin fully prevents sunburn

questions.prompt: Which part of the eye has cells that notice light and color?
choices: The optic nerve that carries signals to the brain
The retina at the back of the eye
The eardrum at the end of the ear canal
The lens at the front that focuses light

questions.prompt: What happens to the eardrum when sound reaches it?
choices: It shakes, and tiny bones pass the shaking inward
It glows, and the light is sent along the nerve
It squeezes, and food is pushed along the ear tube
It freezes, and the hair cells stay perfectly still

questions.prompt: Why does food seem to lack flavor when you have a stuffy nose?
choices: The tongue stops making any taste when you have a cold
Stuffy noses stop the brain from receiving sound signals
Taste buds only work when the nose is full of mucus
Flavor depends on smell and taste working together

questions.prompt: A child goes to many loud concerts without ear protection. What is the likely risk?
choices: Loud noise can cause the retina at the back of the eye to stop sensing light
Loud noise can make the three tiny bones in the ear stronger
Loud noise can permanently damage the hair cells of the inner ear
Loud noise can make the eardrum grow thicker and hear more

questions.prompt: Which of these is caused by a virus?
choices: The common cold, which spreads in tiny droplets
Strep throat, which needs antibiotics to clear
A bruise, which forms when small vessels are hurt
A broken bone, which heals when new bone grows

questions.prompt: How long should you wash your hands with soap and water?
choices: About five seconds, wiping them dry on your shirt
About twenty seconds, scrubbing all over the hands
About two seconds, rinsing with only water and not using any soap
About two minutes, using only very hot water

questions.prompt: A child has a cold and the family asks for antibiotics. Why would a doctor probably say no?
choices: Antibiotics are not strong enough to kill any germ in the body
Colds are not caused by germs, so no medicine could ever help
Colds are caused by viruses, and antibiotics work only on bacteria
Colds are caused by bacteria, and antibiotics work only on viruses

questions.prompt: Which action best stops a sneeze from spreading germs to others?
choices: Sneezing into your bare hand, then touching a doorknob
Sneezing into the air so the droplets travel far away
Sneezing while holding your breath and not telling anyone
Sneezing into your elbow, then washing your hands

questions.prompt: What do antibodies do?
choices: They push food through the long coiled intestine
They send fast messages from the nerves to the brain
They stick to a particular germ and mark it for removal
They carry oxygen from the lungs to every cell in the body

questions.prompt: How does a vaccine help the body?
choices: It destroys every kind of germ that may ever get into the body for life
It replaces white blood cells with stronger and newer ones
It makes the skin thick enough that no germ can get past
It lets the immune system practice on a harmless piece of a germ

questions.prompt: Why do most people catch chicken pox only once?
choices: The immune system remembers the virus and reacts quickly later
The virus is destroyed once the skin has completely healed over
The body makes new bones that no virus is able to enter
The fever from the illness burns away the virus forever

questions.prompt: A child gets a vaccine and has a sore arm for a day. What is the best way to understand it?
choices: It shows the vaccine has damaged the bone beneath the skin
It is a common mild side effect, and the vaccine is still studied for safety
It proves the vaccine has given the child the full disease that it was made to prevent
It means that the immune system has failed and must be restarted

questions.prompt: Which nutrient is mainly used to build and repair muscles and other cells?
choices: Carbohydrate, found in foods like bread, rice and pasta
Calcium, found in foods like yogurt and cheese
Fiber, found in foods like oats and vegetables
Protein, found in foods like beans, eggs and fish
